identity.title: Overthinking Reduction with Decoupled Rewards and Curriculum Data Scheduling

problem.claim: Reduce excessive reasoning length in RLVR-trained reasoning models without reducing task performance.

gap.claim: Existing length-penalty methods can degrade performance because trajectory-level rewards are misaligned with token-level optimization.

contributions.claim: DECS, a framework with decoupled token-level rewards that distinguish and penalize redundant tokens.
A curriculum batch-scheduling strategy intended to balance reasoning efficiency and efficacy.
An analysis identifying two flaws in current length rewards: penalizing essential exploratory tokens and rewarding partial redundancy.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe DECS's decoupled token-level reward mechanism and curriculum scheduling as novel, including the claimed first-of-its-kind characterization of the reward mechanism.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that DECS reduced reasoning tokens by more than 50% across seven benchmarks while maintaining or improving performance.
The authors report that reasoning-efficiency gains were achieved without compromising underlying reasoning power.

narrative_sequence.summary: RLVR-trained reasoning models may overproduce reasoning tokens without performance benefit, limiting practical utility.
Length penalties can hurt performance because trajectory-level rewards do not align with token-level optimization.
The authors identify erroneous penalties on exploratory tokens and inadvertent rewards for partial redundancy.
DECS combines decoupled token-level redundancy penalties with curriculum batch scheduling.
The authors report over 50% token reduction across seven benchmarks with maintained or improved performance.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links failure of length penalties to reward-granularity misalignment and separates exploratory from redundant tokens.

lessons.interpretation: Efficiency objectives may need token-level distinctions that preserve useful search while targeting redundancy.
lessons.application: When proposing a reasoning-efficiency method, define which tokens are useful exploration versus redundancy and align the reward at that granularity.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when token roles cannot be identified reliably or when sequence-level outcomes are the only trustworthy supervision.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify benchmark identities, baseline methods, statistical results, or the conditions under which performance was maintained or improved.
The claimed theoretical discovery and conclusions are author-reported and cannot be independently assessed from the abstract alone.
